name: Russia, My History (VDNKh)
funding: The Humanitarian Projects Foundation runs it and gets most of its money from Gazprom, per RFE/RL in 2019. Gazprom co-financed parks from 2016. Federal and Moscow bodies are partners.
watch: Archimandrite Tikhon Shevkunov heads the foundation's expert council. The Education Ministry recommended the parks as teaching material in 2017.
why_flagged: The Humanitarian Projects Foundation runs it and gets most of its money from Gazprom, per RFE/RL in 2019. Gazprom co-financed parks from 2016. Federal and Moscow bodies are partners.

propaganda.summary: A foundation funded mainly by Gazprom, with the presidential administration as partner, runs the parks. Historian Ivan Kurilla calls them an ideological tool, and Bumaga reported pro-war exhibits in 2023.

name: State Museum of the History of Religion
funding: Federal state museum under the Russian Ministry of Culture since 1991. It moved from Kazan Cathedral to Pochtamtskaya Street 14 in 2000.
watch: Its antireligious displays ended in the 1990s.

propaganda.summary: The USSR Ministry of Culture took over the museum in 1961. Its directors from 1968 to 1987, trained at the Party's atheism institute, built an atheist propaganda programme of lectures and touring exhibitions.

name: VDNKh (Exhibition of Achievements of National Economy)
funding: Owned by the City of Moscow, which took the controlling stake from the federal government after a 2013 decision by Putin, and run as a state joint-stock company.
watch: The 2.4 million square metre site holds about 400 buildings, 49 of them listed heritage; Mayor Sobyanin reports more than 30 million visitors a year.

propaganda.summary: Stalin's government opened the All-Union Agricultural Exhibition on 1 August 1939 to showcase collectivisation; scholars call it the main Stalinist propaganda venue. Renamed VDNKh in 1959, it displayed Soviet economic achievement until 1991.

name: Victory Museum (Central Museum of the Great Patriotic War)
funding: Federal museum under Russia's Ministry of Culture. Its director Alexander Shkolnik was honoured by Putin in 2021 for patriotic education and sanctioned by the UK and Australia in 2022.
watch: Opened on Poklonnaya Hill on 9 May 1995 in Anatoly Polyansky's building; the 2022 exhibition Ordinary Nazism drew 150,000 visitors in its first month.

propaganda.summary: Since April 2022 the federal museum has staged exhibitions such as Ordinary Nazism and Ordinary NATOzism presenting Ukraine's army as heirs of wartime Nazi collaborators, echoing the Kremlin's denazification justification for the invasion.

name: Museum of Yugoslavia
funding: A state institution of Serbia, whose government appoints its director with the Ministry of Culture's consent. Formed in 1996 from the Tito Memorial Centre and the Museum of the Revolution.
watch: Serbia's most visited museum, with 100,000 to 120,000 visitors a year; the complex includes Mihailo Janković's 1962 building and the House of Flowers, Tito's tomb.

propaganda.summary: The City of Belgrade built the museum in 1962 as a 70th birthday gift to Tito, to display and preserve the gifts he received; after his death in 1980 it became the Tito Memorial Centre.

name: Voortrekker Monument
funding: A Section 21 non-profit company since 1993. In 2011 it told Parliament tourism gave 56 to 60 percent of revenue and the state grant, R1,853,000 in 2010, a small share.
watch: Gerard Moerdijk's monument stands in a nature reserve with a 20,000-seat amphitheatre from 1949; retired Major General Gert Opperman led it as CEO from 2000.

propaganda.summary: Inaugurated 16 December 1949 by Prime Minister Malan with mostly government funding, the monument gave the new National Party government a stage to celebrate the volk and articulate white supremacy.

name: Museo de América
funding: Owned by the Spanish General State Administration, one of the national museums attached to the Ministry of Culture, under the education and later culture ministries since its creation.
watch: Created by decree in April 1941, shown in the Archaeological Museum from 1944; its Ciudad Universitaria building part-opened in 1965 and fully in 1994.

propaganda.summary: Franco's Ministry of Education created the museum by decree in 1941 within the Hispanidad ideology; its decree said it should inspire Spaniards and its displays presented conquest and colonisation as a civilising, evangelising project.

name: Ájtte, Swedish Mountain and Sámi Museum
funding: Owned by a foundation of the Swedish state, Norrbotten Region, Jokkmokk Municipality and two Sámi organisations. State money, from a court ruling on hydropower compensation, covered about half its budget in 2009.
watch: The state names the chair and three board members; opened in June 1989 as Sweden's main museum and archive of Sámi culture.
records_note: No budget figures or board list read on its own site.

name: Kin Museum of Contemporary Art (Konstmuseet i Norr)
funding: Norrbotten's county art museum, paid for by Kiruna Municipality and Norrbotten Region. In 2024 it spent SEK 2M more than they gave, counting a withdrawn SEK 2.2M municipal grant as restored.
watch: It sits in Kiruna's new city hall, built with LKAB as client after the iron ore mine forced the town centre to move.
records_note: Visitor numbers and the deficit come from SVT; no annual report or accounts were read.

name: Chiang Kai-shek Memorial Hall
funding: Run and funded from the central budget by an agency of Taiwan's Ministry of Culture, which directs its transformation and negotiated the 2024 honour guard change with the defence ministry.
watch: Built from 31 October 1976 and opened 5 April 1980 with a 6.3 metre bronze statue of Chiang; the changing of the guard draws tourists.

propaganda.summary: Built 1976 to 1980 to commemorate Chiang Kai-shek with a giant statue and military honour guard; the Ministry of Culture began a transitional justice project in 2017 and removed the guard in 2024.
